metadata.title: Smiley v. Citibank (South Dakota), NA, 517 U.S. 735 (1996) (No. 95-860)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Smiley v. Citibank (South Dakota), NA

Opinion filed: 1996-06-10

Docket No.: 95-860

Citations:
• 135 L. Ed. 2d 25
• 116 S. Ct. 1730
• 517 U.S. 735
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 3594

Case holding summaries:
• "[A]ny charges made against [the borrower] in excess of the lawful rate of interest, whether called `fines,' `charges,' `dues,' or `interest,' are in fact interest, and usurious"
• holding, as a matter of federal law, that the courts should "defer to the reasonable judgments of agencies with regard to the meaning of ambiguous terms in statutes that they are charged with administering"
• "Since we have concluded that the Comptroller's regulation deserves deference, the question before us is not whether it represents the best interpretation of the statute, but whether it represents a reasonable one."
• An agency’s “change [in interpretation] is not invalidat- ing, since the whole point of Chevron is to leave the discretion provided by the ambiguities of a statute with the implementing agency.”
• noting the deference due to actions taken pursuant to APA notice-and-comment procedures "designed to assure due deliberation"
• "... [the] whole point of Chevron is to leave the discretion provided by the ambiguities of a statute with the implementing agency."
• "To be sure, agency interpretations that are of long standing come before us with a certain credential of reasonableness, since it is rare that error would long persist. But neither antiquity nor contemporaneity with the statute is a condition of validity."
• noting that Chevron deference is warranted despite a change in position so long as the agency avoids the “pitfalls” of a “[s]udden and unexplained change,” or “change that does not take account of legitimate reliance on prior inter- pretations”
• “Since we due to low prices since December 1, 2001.” H.R. Conf. Rep. have concluded that the Comptroller's regulation deserves No. 107-424 at 446 (2002
• stating that, in certain circumstances, an agency's inconsistent interpretations of a statute are not entitled to deference
• Court accords deference to agencies under Chevron because of a presumption that Congress, "when it left ambiguity in a statute [that was] meant for implementation by an agency, understood that the ambiguity would be resolved, first and foremost by the agency [rather than the courts.]"
• prior contradictory agency position is not fatal
• “Where * * * a court is addressing transactions that occurred at a time when there was no clear agency guidance, it would be absurd to ignore the agency’s current authoritative pronouncement of what the statute means.”
• sustaining Comptroller of the Currency's 1996 regulation promulgated more than 130 years after governing statuteNational Bank Act of 1864was enacted
• "Of course we deny deference to `agency litigating positions that are wholly unsupported by regulations, rulings, or administrative practice.' " (citing Bowen )
• distinguishing between an agency's interpretation of the substantive meaning of a statute and the question of whether a statute is pre-emptive
• expressly not deciding the question of whether a court should defer to an agency's interpretation that a statutory provision, which does not explicitly authorize preemption, nonetheless preempts some state rule
• interest is " 'compensation which is paid by the borrower to the lender or by the debtor to the creditor for ... use [of money]' "
• explaining that “[s]udden and unexplained change” in agency position, or change that “does not take account of legitimate reliance on prior interpretation” may be arbitrary and capricious
• APA notice and comment “designed to assure due deliberation”
• “[C]hange is not invalidating, since the whole point of Chevron is to leave the discretion provided by the ambiguities of a statute with the implementing agency.”
• prior contradictory agency position is not fatal
• distinguishing between the "substantive (as opposed to pre-emptive) meaning of a statute," on which deference must be granted, and "the question of whether a statute is pre-emptive"
• explaining that Chevron deference arises out of background presumptions of congressional intent
• deferring to this interpretation of “interest”
• "It is our practice to defer to the reasonable judgments of agencies with regard to the meaning of ambiguous terms in statutes that they are charged with administering"
• assuming, but not deciding, that "whether a statute is pre-emptive . . . must always be decided de novo by the courts"
• stating that “the question before us is not whether [an agency interpretation] represents the best interpretation of the statute, but whether it represents a reasonable one”
• “[C]hange is not invalidating, since the whole point of Chevron is to leave the discretion provided by the ambiguities of a statute with the implementing agency.”
• "Congress, when it left ambiguity in a statute meant for implementation by an agency, understood the ambiguity would be resolved, first and foremost, by the agency."
• “Of course the mere fact that an agency interpretation contradicts a prior agency position is not fatal.”
• distinguishing between the “substantive (as opposed to pre-emptive) meaning of a statute,” on which deference must be granted, and “the question of whether a statute is pre-emptive”
• an agency's decision to change a policy is valid if not arbitrary, capricious, or an abuse of discretion
• “[C]hange is not invalidating, since the whole point of Chevron is to leave the discretion provided by the ambiguities of a statute with the implementing agency.”
• "Nor does it matter that the regulation was prompted by litigation, including this very suit."
• "[T]he mere fact that an agency interpretation contradicts a prior agency position is not fatal."
• finding that the fact that regulation was issued more than 100 years after statute "makes no difference"
• “Any flat charge may, of course, readily be converted to a percentage charge — which was indeed the basis for 19th century decisions holding that flat charges violated state usury laws establishing maximum ‘rates.’ ”
• An agency's "change [in interpretation] is not invalidating, since the whole point of Chevron is to leave the discretion provided by the ambiguities of a statute with the implementing agency."
• “[C]hange that does not take account of legitimate reliance on prior interpretation . . . may be ‘arbitrary, capricious [or] an abuse of discretion.’”
• “Congress, when it left ambiguity in a statute meant for implementation by an agency, understood the ambiguity would be resolved, first and foremost, by the agency.”
• holding that late fees were interest under the National Bank Act
• giving deference to the regulations of the Comptroller of the Currency
• “[W]e deny deference ‘to agency litigating positions that are wholly unsupported by regulations, rulings, or administrative prac- tice.’ The deliberateness of such positions, if not indeed their authoritativeness, is suspect.”
• “Of course we deny deference to ‘agency litigating positions that are wholly unsupported by regulations, rulings, or administrative prac- tice.’ ” (citing Bowen)
• "To be sure, agency interpretations that are of long standing come before us with a certain credential of reasonableness, since it is rare that error would long persist."
• "[T]he mere fact that an agency interpretation contradicts a prior agency position is not fatal.... [C]hange is not invalidating, since the whole point of Chevron is to leave the discretion provided by the ambiguities of a statute with the implementing agency."
• deferring to OCC under Chevron
• "Nor does it matter that the regulation was prompted by litigation, including this very suit. . . . That it was litigation which disclosed the need for the regulation is irrelevant."
• "[T]he mere fact that an agency interpretation contradicts a prior agency position is not fatal."
